title: Of the Labyrinth
excerpt: A professor visits a student after discovering a disturbing story written in place of an examination answer.
body:
At the October examination session for Medical Physics, the written test consisted of a single open-ended question. The subject was the laws of hydrodynamics. While marking the papers submitted by first-year students (along with a few stragglers from the second and third years, and even, though they were very few, the fourth), the Professor noticed that one of them had written a short story in the space provided for the answer.

The story, which the Professor read with mounting disbelief, was dreadful. Needless to say, it had nothing whatsoever to do with the question or the subject of the examination. There were three characters, two men and a woman, whose behaviour struck the increasingly astonished Professor as utterly incomprehensible. At many points, their actions and thoughts seemed to conceal some kind of shadow, as though they had to be interpreted by turning them into their opposites or deciphering some elaborate code.

The author of what might have been regarded as a prank in very poor taste, or the outward manifestation of profound psychological distress, was an unremarkable student of mediocre appearance, whom the Professor had never had occasion to address during his lectures, either to praise him or, still less, to reprimand him. He was an utterly colourless individual.

Using concern as his pretext, prompted by the appearance of the word *suicide* in the text, the Professor decided to pay the student a visit. As he knocked on the door of the small apartment the student shared with six others, the Professor felt that it was a sense of responsibility that had driven him to intrude upon another person's life, and experienced a sudden surge of entirely unwarranted pride.

The door was opened by a young man whom the Professor had no recollection of ever seeing before.

"Are you Student X?" he asked, his voice barely audible.

"No," the young man replied. "Come, I'll take you to him."

The young man seemed incapable of surprise and, worse still, appeared to know him. The Professor realised that he was afraid, though he could find no explanation for his fear. He was certainly in no danger of losing his life (among other things, the young man was so emaciated and undernourished that a single slap would have been enough to put him out of action), and at any moment he could have invented an excuse and left the apartment, never to set foot in it again. And yet echoes remained of the feeling that had swelled his chest only minutes earlier, that feeling which now struck him as a harmless sin of pride.

He was led into a filthy room, its floor littered with rubbish of every description, dirty clothes and scraps of food. It resembled the lair of a sorrowful predator. The student was sitting there on a small sofa, holding a cup of tea. He barely raised his eyes when he heard the Professor enter. The young man left them alone without a word.

The student looked up at him as though that simple gesture demanded every last ounce of his strength.

"Good evening, Professor," X said. "I've been expecting you."

title: It was September
excerpt: A recently divorced man discovers a mysterious, heretical Bible hidden within the pages of an electric drill’s instruction manual.
body:
About a week after divorcing his second wife, fifty-six-year-old Doug Haskins, perhaps under the influence of a few too many glasses of an excellent artisanal walnut liqueur, found himself leafing through the maintenance manual for his electric drill. He was sprawled on the living room couch in an awkward position, utterly devoid of any semblance of dignity. His poorly shaved face reflected the bluish glow of the television, which was tuned to some random program.
Doug had always loved drills, versatile tools of tremendous power and precision. What he hated (like almost every other human being on the planet) was having to take care of them. In his imagination, shaped by a middle-aged man's life in the Midwest, a drill was something primordial, prehistoric, comparable to a boulder of sandstone, an erupting volcano, or better yet, a volcano that had previously been mistaken for a harmless mountain before suddenly revealing its devastating destructive power.
The idea of having to *care for* a drill in order to keep it working properly made him almost uncomfortable.
At any rate, that evening, for the first time, he began leafing through the manual, and it took him several minutes to realize that what he was reading in the English-language section had nothing to do with the necessary procedures for removing dust and debris from the ventilation openings (perhaps using a can of compressed air).
Or rather, the section began with some generic advice, but at a certain point the sentences (gradually?) began to change, to transmute, their tone shifting from the technical language one would expect of any manual to that of an actual story.
It was the incredible tale of a homeless man who met God in a stairwell in Bloomington.
*Where is Bloomington?* Doug wondered, half asleep. He vaguely remembered a Bloomington in Monroe County.
Surely it couldn't be the same town he had visited several years earlier. The Bloomington in the story was an exotic, surreal little town, and the God whom the protagonist encountered was a tall, dark-skinned individual who developed an ambiguous relationship with him, fraught with strange unspoken implications.
After reading the passage, Doug (now fully awake and, as far as possible, sober) grew curious to see whether the sections in the other languages also concealed similar texts.
He switched on the computer in his study and opened the manual to the French section. With the help of translation software, he discovered that no, this part was not the same at all. It was the continuation, in another language, of the story of the man who met God in the stairwell.
The next section was in German, and there too, despite a few technical difficulties, he managed to read the continuation of the tale, which grew increasingly obscure.
Until, as he went on translating, he came to understand that what he was reading was neither a short story nor a novel, but an actual heretical Bible, full of poetry and an unsuspected,incomprehensible tenderness.
When he had finished reading, Doug went back to lie on the couch, pressing one hand against his tired eyes.
Outside his apartment—or rather, outside the twelve-story apartment building in which his own apartment drowned in the shadows cast by the neighboring buildings, surrounded by a broad expanse of concrete—there was a small garden of violets.
Doug thought of those violets, and of the bees (always different ones) that came to gather their pollen every day, from the very first light of dawn.
With some effort, he got up from the couch and walked over to the living room window.
The garden was still there, but the night was not yet over.
